extracted.intended_audience: members of the public submitting comments on proposed federal regulations (users of Regulations.gov)
extracted.subtask_short: writing public comments on federal regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for members of the public on how to prepare effective written comments for federal rulemaking dockets, including what to include, how to support arguments, procedural reminders, and expectations about agency responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and Understand the Regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective, relevant comments provide regulators with information to help them improve draft rules, and are typically most effective when they provide information directly relevant to analyzing the rule and its potential impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully read the rule text and supporting materials so your comment addresses provisions and impacts that matter to the agency's analysis. Comments that stray from the substance of the rule are less useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Over Quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: A single, well-supported comment may carry more weight than a thousand form letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on mass-produced form letters; prioritize a clear, evidence-based, individual comment over many identical or low-substance submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the Issues with Specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the docket ID number and other identifying information in your subject line, as comments cannot be considered if they are misdirected or get lost because the identifying information was not included. Clearly identify the section(s) of the rule your comment is addressing and make the section you are addressing clear at every point in your comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include docket ID and precise references to the rule text; state which specific section, paragraph, or provision you are addressing and mark this in the subject and throughout the comment to ensure the agency can locate and consider your remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide Specific Arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply stating that you support or oppose a policy is not as persuasive as explaining how the policy would positively or negatively impact the specific situation with which you are familiar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain concretely how the proposed rule affects people, businesses, or operations in real terms; tie claims to facts or examples rather than just expressing general approval or objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't Assume You Need to Be an Expert
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the most effective comments are from individuals who describe the impacts of a proposal in terms of their own lived experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide firsthand accounts and observations about how a rule would affect you or your community; experiential testimony can be valuable even if you lack formal technical expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Specific References
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the page number, column, and/or paragraph from the Federal Register if you are commenting on a particular word, phrase, or sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When challenging or proposing alternate wording, cite precise locations in the published rule so reviewers can see exactly what you mean and verify the context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Relevant Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide relevant data, statistics, or studies to support your comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantiate claims with empirical evidence, citations to authoritative studies, or verifiable statistics to strengthen the persuasiveness and usefulness of your comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularly Influential Comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly influential public comments are often those that simply provide good reasoning and evidence or a perspective that the agency had not previously considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to add novel perspectives or strong analytic reasoning—comments that supply new evidence, novel policy-relevant viewpoints, or clear argumentation are more likely to affect agency decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency Discretion and Expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: While members of the public are allowed and welcome to express their support or opposition to a proposed regulation, an agency is not required to change its proposed policy simply because a commenter suggests it should.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that agencies weigh comments within statutory and policy constraints; framing comments to address legal, factual, or analytical flaws is more useful than mere expressions of preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: A comment that is constructive and provides information to support an argument is more likely to inform the agency's decision-making process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, offer specific alternatives, suggested wording, or practical solutions rather than only criticizing; constructive proposals help agencies consider how to revise rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet Submission Deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments must be submitted by the deadline (11:59 PM Eastern on the deadline date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm and respect the docket's deadline—late comments may not be considered. Note the exact time zone and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submissions Become Part of the Public Record
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions become part of the public record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include confidential or sensitive personal information in comments; everything submitted may be viewable by others and retained in the docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies Must Consider Relevant Matter Presented
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider all 'relevant matter presented' but are not required to respond to every comment individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide relevant, on-point information to increase the likelihood your comment is considered; recognize that agencies summarize and synthesize comments rather than replying to each one line-by-line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form Letters Typically Count as One Comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Form letters typically count as one comment regardless of how many people send them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a form letter, be aware it may be treated as a single submission for counting purposes; individualized substance is more influential than volume of identical submissions.
